stories.title: Kazakhstan parliamentary elections begin: What’s at stake?
stories.summary: The Central Asian country heads to the polls on August 23. Kazakhstan heads to the polls this week in a snap parliamentary election that is expected to strengthen President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s rule over the country. The last parliamentary elections were in 2023. The election comes just weeks after Kazakhstan, a nation of 21 million that borders Russia and China, revamped its legislative system by introducing constitutional changes and shifting from a dual-chamber parliament to a single-chamber one as it seeks to assert itself as a major democratic power in Central Asia. How does the election process work and what’s at stake? When is the election happening? Elections for the 145 seats of the Kurultai, the country’s new unicameral legislature, will take place on August 23. To enter government, parties must receive at least 5 percent of the overall vote. Before July 1, when Kazakhstan’s new constitutional system came into effect, the parliament was bicameral, with the Mazhilis (lower house) and Senate (upper house). On the day the new system came into effect, President Tokayev signed a decree calling the snap election. According to national media outlet Astana Times, under the previous system, “legislation passed through the Mazhilis before moving to the Senate. Under the new model, the Kurultai concentrates legislative consideration, and adopted laws are then sent to the President.”

stories.title: Canadian PM Carney says new US tariffs are 'designed to hurt us and divide us'
stories.summary: "We cannot accept what they've offered, and we will not give what they've asked," Carney said during a speech outlining Canada's position on the trade dispute with the US. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has hit out at new US tariffs on Canada, saying they were "designed to hurt us and divide us" after talks between Ottawa and Washington broke down on Friday. Sharing further details on why Canada walked away from what he called a "bad deal," Carney said: "We cannot accept what they've offered, and we will not give what they've asked." Duties impacting around $20 billion worth of Canadian goods took effect on Saturday after the two countries failed to come to an agreement on a trade deal, with both sides accusing each other of trying to implement last-minute changes. He also warned that Ottawa would match US tariffs "dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses." The Office of the United States Trade Representative has described it as a "missed opportunity" for Canada, which it said was maintaining a "prolonged retaliation" against the US. "Despite the U.S. offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days," it added in a statement posted on social media. The breakdown in talks came despite optimism from US President Donald Trump that a deal could be reached. Trump had postponed the initial planned start date of the tariffs from Wednesday as an agreement appeared near. Trump, who has repeatedly suggested that Canada should become the US' "51st state," said early on Sunday that Ottawa wanted "the benefits of being a State, without being one." "They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!!," he added.
